lessons.title: A Side-by-Side Risk-Return Scorecard of Indian Asset Classes

children.text: You now have every piece you need. Chapter 2 gave you the risks volatility misses. Chapter 3 built the traditional benchmarks. Chapter 4 profiled each alternative. The first two lessons of Chapter 5 turned headline returns into real, post-tax returns. This lesson puts it all on one page: a scorecard that lines up ten Indian asset classes across the dimensions that actually matter, then shows how the "best" asset changes completely depending on who is investing. Keep it. It is the tool you will use on every new product pitch you ever receive.

body.text: There is no best asset class, only the best fit for a particular investor. A scorecard does not pick winners. It makes trade-offs visible, so you can weight them by what your own life demands.

children.text: The Facts Behind the Scores

body.caption: Ten Indian asset classes: the key facts from this course (illustrative, for a 30% slab investor with 5% inflation)

body.title: Illustrative real, post-tax annual return for a 30% slab investor (%)

body.text: Return alone would put the PE fund first. But it earns only about 1 point more than an index fund in this illustration, with a decade of lock-in, a J-curve, appraisal-based values and the widest manager dispersion of any asset class. The scorecard exists to stop that single number from making the decision.

children.text: The Scorecard

Each asset is scored from 1 (worst) to 5 (best) on seven dimensions. The scores are judgements based on the facts above and the lessons of this course, not precise measurements. Reasonable people could move any score by a point.
Real return:
expected return after fees, costs, tax and inflation.
Downside protection:
how badly it can hurt in a bad year, including losses hidden by appraisal.
Liquidity:
how quickly you can get cash at a fair price.
Transparency:
how reliable and frequent the valuation and disclosure are.
Low cost:
fees, transaction costs and tax drag combined.
Diversifies Indian equity:
how differently it behaves from the Nifty, especially in crises.
Access:
how easy it is to start, and to invest a sensible amount without concentration.

body.caption: Risk-return scorecard of Indian asset classes (1 = worst, 5 = best; illustrative judgements)

children.text: Two warnings about reading the totals. First, the Nifty index fund scores 1 on diversifying Indian equity because it is Indian equity. That is not a flaw; it is the core that other assets diversify around. Second, crypto's high liquidity and access scores do not cancel its extreme downside. A simple total treats every dimension as equally important, and for almost no investor are they.
Weighting the Scorecard for Real People

body.caption: w = the weight you give each dimension, s = the asset's score on it
Two investors, two sets of weights
headers: Mrs Rao, 64, retired, needs regular income

body.title: Weighted scores out of 5 for two different investors (illustrative)

children.text: For Mrs Rao, the FD is the top scorer and every locked-up alternative sinks below 2. For Vivek, the FD drops behind gold and the index fund, and the PE fund climbs above the other locked-up alternatives, although it still trails all four traditional assets. That is the real lesson. A scorecard ranks nothing until you tell it who is investing, and even for a long-horizon investor, most alternatives only make sense as satellites around a traditional core.

body.title: Calculate a weighted score
body.prompt: An investor weights only three dimensions: real return 50%, liquidity 30% and downside protection 20%. An asset scores 3 on real return, 4 on liquidity and 5 on downside protection. What is its weighted score out of 5?
body.explanation: 0.50 × 3 + 0.30 × 4 + 0.20 × 5 = 1.5 + 1.2 + 1.0 = 3.7. Change the weights to favour return and the score falls; favour safety and it rises, even though the asset itself has not changed.

body.title: Where alternatives genuinely add something, and where they mostly repackage

columns.label: Genuine additions for the right investor
points: Gold: a proven crisis diversifier at low cost
Listed REITs: diversified property income with daily liquidity
PE and VC: exposure to companies not yet listed, for those with the capital, horizon and access
High-quality private credit: a modest income premium for money that can be locked away

columns.label: Mostly repackaged risk
points: Pre-IPO shares and small angel portfolios: equity risk with worse liquidity and odds
Low-quality credit and P2P: equity-like downside for fixed-income-like upside
A leveraged second flat: concentrated, illiquid, and often below fixed income after costs
Crypto as a core holding: extreme volatility with no cash-flow anchor

body.title: Reading the scorecard
body.question: Why does the same PE fund score about 1.8 for a retiree and about 2.4 for a 35-year-old long-horizon investor?
options: Because the PE fund's actual returns are different for younger investors
Because the two investors weight the dimensions differently: the retiree cares far more about liquidity and downside, where PE scores poorly
Because SEBI allows younger investors better terms in AIFs
Because the scorecard contains a calculation error
body.explanation: The asset's scores are identical for both. Only the weights change. The retiree puts 55% of her weight on downside protection and liquidity, where PE scores 2 and 1, while the younger investor puts 35% on real return, where PE scores 4.

body.title: Score a new pitch
body.scenario: A wealth manager pitches an SM REIT to Vivek. It holds a single pre-leased warehouse near Chennai, leased to one logistics company for nine more years. Minimum investment is ₹10 lakh. The distribution yield is 8.5%, taxed mostly at slab rates. Units are listed on BSE but rarely trade. A registered valuer values the warehouse periodically.
body.prompt: Score this product from 1 to 5 on each of the seven dimensions, and compare it with a listed office REIT on the scorecard.
body.modelAnswer:
Suggested scores (reasonable people may differ by a point):
- Real return: 2. An 8.5% yield taxed at 31.2% is about 5.8% after tax, and with little growth from one fixed lease, roughly 1% real, before any vacancy.
- Downside protection: 2. One tenant and one building: if the tenant leaves, income can fall to zero.
- Liquidity: 2. Listed, but rarely traded, so selling at a fair price may be slow.
- Transparency: 3. Periodic valuation and regulated disclosure, but no active market price to cross-check.
- Low cost: 3. Management fees and slab taxation drag on the headline yield.
- Diversifies Indian equity: 3. Contracted rent behaves differently from equity, although warehouse demand still depends on the economy.
- Access: 3. ₹10 lakh is a high minimum for a single-asset exposure.
Total: 18 out of 35.

Compared with the listed office REIT (26 out of 35), the SM REIT offers a higher headline yield but scores lower on downside protection, liquidity, transparency and access, mainly because of single-asset, single-tenant concentration. For Vivek, it could only make sense as a small satellite, not as a replacement for a diversified listed REIT.

body.title: Build a scorecard for any new product
steps: Convert the headline return to a real, post-tax return using your own tax bracket
Find the worst realistic outcome, including a stress year and losses hidden by appraisal
Establish the time to cash and whether early exit is allowed, and at what discount
Identify who sets the value, how often, and whether there is a live market price
Add up every fee, transaction cost and the tax drag
Ask what drives its cash flows, and whether that is really different from Indian equity
Check the minimum ticket against the size of your total portfolio
Weight the seven scores by your own goals, horizon and income needs before comparing

points: A scorecard makes trade-offs visible across seven dimensions: real return, downside protection, liquidity, transparency, cost, diversification and access.
On an unweighted basis, FDs, gold ETFs, index funds and listed REITs score highest, while locked-up alternatives cluster at the bottom.
Return alone would rank the PE fund first, but its roughly 1-point real edge over an index fund comes with a decade of lock-in and wide manager dispersion.
Weights change the answer: an FD tops the list for a retiree, while gold and index funds lead for a long-horizon investor.
Even for long-horizon investors, most alternatives score best as satellites around a traditional core, not as replacements for it.
Use the eight-step checklist to score any new product before comparing it with what you already own.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice or a recommendation to buy or avoid any asset class or product. Scores are illustrative judgements, and return figures are illustrative assumptions from earlier lessons. Individual products within an asset class can differ widely. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
